t: Second Largest Digit in a String — Track Two Champions in One Pass
o:
## Understanding the problem

The string mixes lowercase letters with digits; among the DISTINCT digits that appear we return the second largest, or −1 when fewer than two distinct values exist. Distinctness is the trap: "abc1111" contains four digit characters but only the value 1, so there is no runner-up despite plenty of digits.

**Example walkthrough:** "dfa12321afd" contains digits {1, 2, 3} — the second largest is 2. "abc1111" contains only {1} — answer −1.

With length ≤ 500 nearly anything passes, but the idiomatic solutions are (a) collect the distinct digits into a set — never more than ten entries — and select, or (b) sweep once tracking the largest and second-largest distinct values. Both are O(n); option (b) generalizes to streams and unbounded inputs, which is the usual follow-up direction.
k: Distinctness drives everything: duplicates of the maximum do NOT create a runner-up ("abc1111" returns −1).
There are only ten digit values, so collecting distinct digits is constant space in practice.
The classic top-two scan promotes on strictly greater and accepts a new second only when first > d > second — the strict inequalities are what block duplicate maxima.

a.n: Approach 1: Collect distinct digits, then select
a.i: Filter digit characters into a set — deduplication comes free — and if at least two values survive, return the second largest by sorting the tiny collection or scanning it. The simplest correct program; the set never exceeds ten elements so selection cost is negligible.
s: Scan s, collecting characters between ‘0’ and ‘9’ into a set.
If fewer than two distinct digits exist, return −1.
Otherwise return the second-largest element (sort and take index 1 from the top, or equivalent).
a.t: O(n) — one pass to collect; selecting among at most 10 values is constant time
a.sp: O(1) — the set holds at most 10 digits

a.n: Approach 2: Single pass tracking the top two distinct values
a.i: Maintain first (largest distinct digit) and second (runner-up), both starting at −1, the natural "missing" sentinel since digits are non-negative. For each digit d: d > first promotes d and demotes old first into second; otherwise second absorbs d only when first > d > second, and those strict inequalities are precisely what stops duplicates of the maximum from polluting second. Stream-friendly, allocation-free, and worth memorizing as the canonical top-k-distinct template.
s: For each character, skip non-digits and parse the numeric value d.
If d > first, shift: second = first, first = d.
Else if first > d > second, set second = d.
a.t: O(n) — a single scan with constant work per character
a.sp: O(1) — two integers regardless of input size

## Wrap-up

Open by restating the distinctness requirement with the "abc1111" example — that is exactly where implementations break. Either approach passes here; volunteering the two-variable scan signals stream-readiness.

**Common pitfalls**

- Counting occurrences instead of distinct values — returning 1 for "abc1111".
- Letting an equal maximum overwrite second: the guard must be strict (d < first AND d > second).
- Forgetting that letters interleave anywhere and that 0 is a legitimate smallest digit.
- Initializing trackers to 0 instead of −1 makes "missing" indistinguishable from an actual 0.

**Likely follow-ups:** k-th largest distinct digit, second most frequent digit, or computing it with a single pass over a data stream too big for memory.
